Commenter says they appreciate SerpApi's product regardless of legality: it provides a machine interface to Google results that Google itself refuses to offer, plus visibility into SERPs that users should have.
Several commenters argue SerpApi only exists because Google doesn't offer a usable, reasonably priced search API: "If google provided a useable reasonably priced API, then SerpApi wouldn't exist."

One commenter hadn't heard of SerpApi before the lawsuit but would now pick it for Google results, since it was apparently so hard for Google to block that Google sued instead. They also noted the advertised "legal shield" where SerpApi assumes scraping liability for customers.

Commenter says people naturally end up using SerpApi or similar search APIs for programmatic search because "they are great for the job," especially when scripts or AI tools search on a user's behalf.

Commenter describes a planned workaround: use SerpApi to save the top 10-20 links for millions of queries into a RAG database. A local LLM and crawler could then do web search without touching Google, with the index refreshed every few months.

Critics in the thread say SerpApi doesn't obey robots.txt the way Google does. One called its traffic "malicious requests to google.com." Another described the issue as pulling far more data from Google, more often, than an indexing operation would need.

A former API user said the most interesting part of SerpApi is its plan-level legal protection. As an example they cited Production at $150 for 15,000 searches/month with a "U.S. Legal Shield." They suspect some companies use SerpApi just for that liability shield.

Skeptics compared the Legal Shield to old SSL certificate warranties: "pretty words, but meaningless in practice." They see the "unless your usage is illegal" clause as a big loophole, e.g. if scraping Google results were ruled copyright infringement.

User complaint about the SerpApi MCP server: embedding the API key in the URL complicates secret management, and they asked for header-based auth settable via an environment variable. In reply, Bearer token auth was said to already work on the /mcp path.

After the dismissal of Google's suit, a commenter predicted SerpApi won't prevail long-term, in court or in the marketplace. They think the dismissal hinged on a fixable DRM-authorization gap and that Google could refile a more airtight case.
